ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Neurology (multiple sclerosis) Consultation — Barbara Jordan

code.originalText: Two-week review with MRI of the brain and spine and the neurology (multiple sclerosis) consultation; vaccines before therapy

text.paragraph: Multiple sclerosis diagnosed elsewhere in a 44-year-old professor and public speaker who walks with a cane, with records of the original evaluation not available. Please confirm and classify the disease on the MRI booked for the morning of your visit, and advise on disease-modifying therapy, its screening and monitoring, vaccination, symptom care and MRI follow-up. [S]
Urgency: Within two weeks, on the same day as her two-week primary care visit. [S]

list.item: Does she meet the 2017 McDonald criteria, and is her course relapsing or progressive, active or not active?
Which disease-modifying therapy, if any, do you advise, and why?
What screening and vaccination are needed before the first dose, and how long before?
What monitoring will the therapy need?
When should the MRI be repeated, and with what protocol?
What do you advise for spasticity, bladder urgency, fatigue and heat sensitivity?
How should she recognize and report a relapse?

text.paragraph: Ms. Jordan, a 44-year-old professor and public speaker, is seen at the request of Dr. Moss. She was told years ago that she had multiple sclerosis; the records are not available. She describes slowly worsening walking over several years, needing a cane for some time, with no attack of new symptoms over days that then recovered. She has leg stiffness, afternoon fatigue, heat sensitivity, urinary urgency and nocturia, and no visual loss or double vision. She has had steroid courses in the past and no disease-modifying therapy. She wants to know whether a treatment can slow the disease, and wants to keep teaching and speaking. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Barbara Jordan was born on February 21, 1936, in Houston, Texas, the youngest of three daughters, and grew up in Houston's Fifth Ward. She graduated magna cum laude from Texas Southern University in 1956 and earned a law degree from Boston University in 1959. [D]

In 1966 she was elected to the Texas Senate, the first Black state senator since 1883. In 1972 she was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives from Houston, the first Black woman from a Southern state to serve in Congress. As a member of the House Judiciary Committee during the 1974 impeachment hearings she said, "My faith in the Constitution is whole, it is complete, it is total." [D]
In 1976 she gave the keynote address at the Democratic National Convention, the first woman and the first African American to do so. [D]

She did not seek a fourth term and left the House in 1979, downplaying reports about her poor health and citing her "internal compass." She became the Lyndon Baines Johnson Public Service Professor at the LBJ School of Public Affairs of the University of Texas at Austin, where she taught until the early 1990s. [D]

In her later years in the House she walked with a cane, which she attributed at the time to "a bum knee"; a disability-press account written after her death says this was the first adaptive equipment her multiple sclerosis required, and that she did not openly acknowledge the disease for years. [D]

It was later revealed that she had been diagnosed with multiple sclerosis around the time she left Congress. The year of the diagnosis is not stated in the obituaries and reference works consulted. [D]

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Active primary progressive multiple sclerosis (G35.B1). More than a year of gradually worsening disability without relapses, with T2 lesions in characteristic brain regions and two or more spinal cord lesions, meets the 2017 McDonald criteria for primary progressive multiple sclerosis without the need for spinal fluid. The enhancing lesion shows inflammatory activity, so the disease is active. B12, thyroid and HIV results and the absence of cord compression exclude the main mimics. At 44, still walking with a cane, with an enhancing lesion, she is the kind of patient most likely to benefit from therapy. [S]
Spastic gait and fall risk (R26.89). Spasticity contributes to her slowness and stiffness; strength is fairly preserved, so a careful baclofen titration should not weaken her. [S]
Neurogenic bladder (N31.9). Urgency with a low residual; safe to treat with a bladder-relaxing medicine, preferably one without anticholinergic effects on concentration. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Moss's intake note and results: blood count, kidney and liver tests, TSH, vitamin B12 and immunoglobulins normal; 25-hydroxyvitamin D 17 ng/mL; JC virus antibody index 0.14, negative. Results since intake: hepatitis B surface antigen, core antibody and surface antibody negative; varicella IgG and measles, mumps and rubella IgG positive; tuberculosis blood test, HIV and hepatitis C negative. MRI this morning, brain with gadolinium: fourteen T2 lesions, periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial in the pons and left middle cerebellar peduncle, with one enhancing right periventricular lesion. Cervical and thoracic spine: three cord lesions at C3, C5 and T6, each shorter than two segments, with no compression. [S]

list.item: Ocrelizumab, the therapy with evidence for primary progressive multiple sclerosis: 300 mg intravenously on day 1 and day 15, then 600 mg every 6 months, with methylprednisolone 100 mg, an antihistamine and acetaminophen beforehand and at least one hour of observation; twice-yearly infusions suit her teaching and travel. [S]

Before the first dose: she is not infected with hepatitis B but not immune, so hepatitis B vaccine; PCV20, recombinant zoster vaccine (two doses, the second after about a month), and Tdap; inactivated vaccines at least two weeks before the first dose and live vaccines at least four weeks before (none needed, as she is immune to varicella and measles); confirm no active infection on each infusion day. [S]

Monitoring: blood count with lymphocytes, liver tests and immunoglobulins before each dose; hepatitis B surface antibody after the series; prompt review of infections, persistent diarrhea or new neurological symptoms; standard breast cancer screening; no live vaccines during treatment; seasonal influenza and COVID-19 vaccines, ideally at least two weeks before an infusion. [S]
MRI: a re-baseline brain MRI three to six months after the first dose, then yearly, on the same scanner where possible and without routine gadolinium; spinal MRI only for new spinal symptoms. [S]
Spasticity: baclofen 5 mg three times a day, increasing to 10 mg three times a day once tolerated, with daily stretching and physical therapy; gabapentin is the second choice if baclofen fails. [S]
Bladder: mirabegron 25 mg daily with timed voiding and a blood pressure check at each visit. [S]
Fatigue and heat: pacing, morning teaching where she chooses, cooling garments and air conditioning, and aerobic exercise in cool water; no fatigue medicine for now. [S]

Relapse plan: new or worsening symptoms lasting more than 24 hours without fever or heat mean a same-day call; check for urinary infection first; heat or infection can bring back old symptoms for hours without new disease activity. [S]
Multiple sclerosis neurology review after the re-baseline MRI and then every six months. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Moss, who sees her the same day. The plan was explained to Ms. Jordan, who agreed and decides who else receives this note; her reproductive plans were discussed privately and recorded in the confidential part of the chart. [S]
Follow-up: Review after the re-baseline MRI, about seven months from now, then every six months; Dr. Moss continues primary care, vaccination and monitoring between visits. [S]
